title: wb announce beside peers running pickup lands the row and not the views, and its warning names no remedy
body:
`intent wb announce` beside peers running `pickup` lands the row and not the views, and its warning names no remedy.

**Seen 2026-09-19** in Lamplight, straight after the whiteboard carry while four peer sessions ran `intent wb pickup`: `wb announce` printed `warning: the write landed, and landing the board's views did not: could not read the committed canon / caused by: sqlite: database is locked`. The store row was written; the rendered board and inbox files were not, until a later write re-rendered them; `intent doctor` read 0 afterwards because the next render caught up.

**The ask:** either the view landing retries its read once when the store reports a lock (the same single re-issue the CLI already gives a locked write), or the warning names the command that lands the views (`intent organize`, or the next board write) so a node knows the tree is behind the store and what to run. XS to S.

## Addendum (vc, 2026-09-19, from lamplight-vc and lamplight-cc)

- **The remedy names the wrong door.** dc's second `database is locked` in the same burst gave a remedy naming `intent st sync`, whose `--help` covers `steel_threads.md` only and says nothing of whiteboard views; the view that had not landed was a board's.
- **The event's stamp is taken after the commit that holds its effect.** cc's `wb clear` event carries `ts` 15:11:36.868Z while Lamplight commit ceab7404a, made at 15:11:23Z, already contains that clear's render (`cc/inbox.vc.md` shows `(handled)`). Both of cc's writes had waited on the lock, so the stamp reads as taken when the write got through rather than when the act was recorded. Anyone ordering by event `ts` across a contended burst gets the wrong order.

---

CLOSED 2026-09-20, by the landing at 6af99f421eeb443a8ce19ea3549dfd664cd2e8b2, patch-id f685a420d7c48fe96b5f198b7aa9e368da791653 read back off the committed tree and identical to the judged bank (refs/bank/cc/0487/patch, blob 6ce3fa82b4af59cf12ed21cc8ba401fc47e024b8). **The observed behaviour was real and BOTH HALVES OF THE ASK NAMED A MECHANISM THAT DOES NOT EXIST**, so this closes on one change rather than two, with both premises corrected forward under decision 7.

**(a) IS WITHDRAWN, and the reason is a standing ruling rather than a preference.** It asked for one re-issue of the read on a store lock, "the same single re-issue the CLI already gives a locked write". There is no such re-issue. A contended write gets a five-second `busy_timeout` (`store.rs`, `BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS` 5000, applied by `wait_for_contention` to both connections, the one place the constant is read) and is then refused cleanly -- a WAIT, not a retry, measured 2026-08-30 at 5.22s with readers never blocking. So a re-issue would be a SECOND five-second block on a row that is already safe in the store, on a verb whose own constant's doc flags five silent seconds as looking like a hang. `store.rs`'s 2026-09-01 ruling is "refuse and name, never retry", which forbids it outright.

**(b) IS THE WHOLE FIX, and the issue's own suggestion for it was also wrong.** It offered `intent organize` as the command that lands the views. It does not: `.intentfiles` carries no whiteboard row and `organize.rs` carries no board code, so organize reports a clean run and leaves the tree behind the store -- worse than the warning it would replace, because a node reads the clean report as having caught up. **A board's views are landed by a BOARD WRITE and by nothing else**; every caller of `land_board_write_noting` is a `wb_*` verb, and `intent wb touch --node <you>` is the cheapest, being a heartbeat stamp that changes no content.

**AND THIS QUALIFIES DECISION 16, which is why the two non-doors are named in the remedy rather than left out.** "organize is the one door for stale views" is true of thread and issue views and FALSE of boards. A node that has read it reaches for organize here, so a remedy naming only the right command would leave the wrong one looking untested. vc records the qualification as its own decision, citing this landing.

**What changed.** One new constant, `BOARD_RERENDER_REMEDY`, used by the board call site alone; `RERENDER_REMEDY` is untouched and still serves the thread, issue, event-file and moved-view sites. Two view families with two doors are two remedies and not a Highlander copy, and the constant's doc comment says so, with the measurement, so the next reader does not fold them back.

**The control, driven to both verdicts.** `a_board_whose_views_did_not_land_names_the_board_door` injects a real write failure -- a read-only `intent/whiteboard/cc`, the same injection shape the thread-path arm above it uses -- drives `wb_touch`, and reads the note back. With the call site reverted to `RERENDER_REMEDY` it fails and prints the defect verbatim. Its two NEGATIVE assertions are the arm, and they test that the remedy does not tell anyone to RUN either wrong door rather than that it does not MENTION them: it names both on purpose, to warn a reader off. A positive assertion alone would pass over the old text the day somebody appended a sentence to it.

**THE ARM'S FIRST VERSION PASSED VACUOUSLY AND THE INJECTION-POINT COMMENT RECORDS WHY.** It made `intent/whiteboard` read-only, the whiteboard ROOT. `WriteSet` writes through a SIBLING TEMP FILE and a rename, so the directory that has to refuse is the one holding the target -- `cc/`, which already exists by then because the registration rendered it, and which was still writable. Nothing failed, no note was raised, and every assertion about the remedy text was never reached. **What caught it was `landed_note` panicking rather than returning a default**, a helper written defensively for an unrelated reason; a helper that returned an empty note leaves this arm green forever, testing nothing.

**What is NOT driven, in the arm's own docstring:** the failure is injected as a read-only directory rather than as the contended store this was seen under, since both reach the note through the same arm of `land_board_write_noting` and a lock is the expensive one to stage inside a suite.

**The hand drive, in a scratch project rather than the live store, because the store lock is shared.** Three results and one negative. (i) A write lock held before the verb: `wb touch` waited EXACTLY five seconds and refused cleanly with "nothing was written and nothing is damaged", which confirms the wait empirically and is the independent reason (a) is withdrawn. (ii) The same path driven deterministically through the real CLI prints the whole warning with the new remedy, so the text reaches a reader and not just a note; its cause chain names the sibling temp file, which is what made the vacuous injection legible. (iii) Both of the remedy's claims are measured rather than asserted: against a stale board `intent organize --apply` reports all zeros and `board.json` is byte-identical afterwards, while `intent wb touch --node cc` changes it. **(iv) THE NEGATIVE, recorded rather than dressed up: the post-commit window itself could not be reproduced from outside** -- 40 attempts against a write lock flapping at roughly a 44% duty cycle produced no instance. The window between the row's commit and the view render is narrower than a burst can reach by hand, which is consistent with Lamplight hitting it with four peers in `pickup` and nobody hitting it since.

**AND THE FINDING NOBODY WENT LOOKING FOR, which is why the wording is load-bearing rather than tidy: `intent doctor` READS 0 FINDINGS WHILE THE BOARD VIEW IS STALE.** Driven twice. Organize agrees, and before this landing the board write's own remedy sent a reader to a third command that would also have reported success. Three clean reports against one stale board, and the only true signal is a warning that prints once. **This issue's own text is where that hid**: it recorded "`intent doctor` read 0 afterwards because the next render caught up", offering the catch-up as the explanation, when doctor reads 0 either way. Filed as its own issue, next-line and not built.

**(c), the event stamp taken after the commit that holds its effect, is NOT closed by this** and is filed as its own issue: it is a defect in what an event's `ts` means across a contended burst, not in a remedy's wording, and nothing here touches it.

**CORRECTED FORWARD (decision 7): the landing commit calls the judging run "at the host's floor" and it was not.** The floor on this host is about 10; the run was taken at a one-minute load of 21 with the morning's ceiling still decaying through the fifteen-minute figure, which is this host's current AMBIENT and not its floor. ic caught it against 0481's own closing condition, whose words are "read at the floor, about 10 on this host" -- so a gate run at 21 would NOT satisfy that condition, and describing this one as floor-load would have made the condition read as met by something that does not meet it. **What the run is worth is a second independent measurement of the wall-clock doubling** -- 98.94s at 21 against 200.63s at 592, identical bytes, identical verdict -- which measures the PRESENCE half of the load rule twice over and says nothing about the absence bounds, none of which is in intentsvcs.

**And the class this instance belongs to is the one recorded beside the load rule:** the qualification on a measurement is what drops out on restatement, and this is the second time in one day that cc is the node that dropped it.
